content: The Alere Determine™ TB LAM Ag rapid assay, introduced by Alere Inc. (USA) in 2012, is a lateral flow immunochromatographic strip test designed to detect the lipoarabinomannan (LAM) antigen in urine. This test uses a polyclonal antibody capture and detection method on a nitrocellulose strip. It is important to note that while the assay is specific for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), it can also detect other non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTMs). LAM, a component of the mycobacterial cell wall, is excreted in urine during mycobacterial infections, making it detectable through this test. The assay requires only a 60 μL urine sample and does not necessitate additional tools or equipment. Results are visually interpreted on the test strip after a 25-minute incubation period. The test is particularly advantageous in resource-limited settings due to its ease of use and minimal infrastructure requirements. The Alere LAM assay is being considered as a diagnostic tool for tuberculosis (TB) in people living with HIV (PLHIV), especially in combination with existing diagnostic methods. The World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned a systematic review to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the Alere LAM assay for TB in PLHIV, as part of efforts to update guidelines for its use. The review included 15 studies conducted in high TB/HIV burden countries, involving 6,814 participants, of whom 26% had TB. The studies assessed the test's accuracy in both symptomatic and unselected populations, with results stratified by inpatient and outpatient settings, as well as by CD4 cell count. For HIV-positive adults with signs and symptoms of TB, the diagnostic accuracy of the Alere LAM assay was as follows: In inpatient settings: sensitivity 52% (40–64%) and specificity 87% (78–93%). In outpatient settings: sensitivity 29% (17–47%) and specificity 96% (91–99%). Across all settings: sensitivity 42% (31–55%) and specificity 91% (85–95%). For HIV-positive adults irrespective of TB symptoms, the diagnostic accuracy was: In inpatient settings: sensitivity 62% (41–83%) and specificity 84% (48–96%). In outpatient settings: sensitivity 31% (18–47%) and specificity 95% (87–99%). Across all settings: sensitivity 35% (22–50%) and specificity 95% (89–98%). For adults with advanced HIV disease (CD4 ≤ 200), the test showed: In inpatient settings: sensitivity 64% (35–87%) and specificity 82% (67–93%). In outpatient settings: sensitivity 21% (8–48%) and specificity 96% (89–99%). Across all settings: sensitivity 26% (9–56%) and specificity 96% (87–98%). For children living with HIV, limited data suggest the following diagnostic accuracy: Sensitivity ranged from 42% to 56%, and specificity ranged from 80% to 95%, depending on the study and setting. The Alere LAM assay has been recognized for its potential to address diagnostic challenges in populations where TB is difficult to diagnose, such as PLHIV with low CD4 counts or advanced disease. The test's reliance on urine as a specimen, rather than sputum, is a significant advantage, as urine is easier and safer to collect. However, challenges such as stock-outs, limited shelf life, and delays in treatment initiation despite rapid test results have been noted. WHO guidelines recommend the use of the Alere LAM assay in specific populations, including: Inpatients with advanced HIV disease or serious illness, irrespective of TB symptoms. Outpatients with CD4 counts <100, irrespective of TB symptoms. The test is not recommended for use in HIV-positive individuals without TB symptoms and with CD4 counts ≥200. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of LAM-based tests, evaluate their use in children and asymptomatic individuals, and assess their cost-effectiveness and integration into routine clinical care.
